content:
A 20-year-old co-pilot who earned her private pilot's license at 17, before she had a driver's license, was among the nine people killed when a Learjet 60 crashed in Florida on Sunday, November 1, 2026.

Her name was Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras. Her mother and stepfather confirmed to the New York Post that she was serving as co-pilot aboard the flight.

The aircraft departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Around 12:50 p.m. local time, the Learjet 60 crashed in a residential area near Greenacres in Palm Beach County, Florida, the FAA said. All nine people aboard were killed.

Filgueiras grew up in Palm Beach County. She earned her private pilot's license at 17 while attending West Boca Raton High School, before she had obtained a driver's license, according to the Palm Beach Post. Her dream was to become a commercial airline pilot.

Authorities have not released the names of the other eight people aboard. The FAA said the National Transportation Safety Board is in charge of the investigation and will provide updates. The cause of the crash has not yet been determined.

Rest in peace, Nathalia.

Update — November 2, 2026

The families of the seven passengers issued a joint statement on November 2 naming them as Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, their friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and the children's nanny, Anita Maria Apellido Cetina, the Palm Beach Post and CNN reported. With co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras already identified by her family, eight of the nine people aboard have now been publicly identified by family members; authorities have not officially released names. At a November 2 news conference, National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said there is some evidence the aircraft was breaking up before impact, and that the crew's report of ice and sub-zero temperatures will be a major focus of the inquiry, according to the Palm Beach Post. The crew reported light, clear ice and moderate turbulence, requested to climb 2,000 feet, and declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude, the NTSB said. One person on the ground suffered a minor leg injury from debris, and close to 600 people near the site were temporarily displaced, officials said. The NTSB said it expects to release a preliminary report within 30 days. The cause of the crash has not been determined.

Update — November 3, 2026

At a November 3 news conference, National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said most of the Learjet's left elevator had been recovered in three pieces between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the impact site, according to the Associated Press. Investigators had not established whether the separation caused the aircraft to lose control or resulted from forces during the descent, Chapman said. The cause of the crash remains undetermined, and the NTSB still expects a preliminary report within 30 days.

Update — November 5, 2026

On November 5, the National Transportation Safety Board said investigators excavating the impact crater had found “a portion of one engine,” and that debris had also turned up on the roofs of homes and buildings near the crash site, according to the agency's update reported by USA Today and PEOPLE. The board asked anyone who finds debris from the Learjet 60 crash not to keep, move, or dispose of it, and to contact the NTSB at witness@ntsb.gov, preferably with a photograph. All recovered wreckage will be taken to a secure location for further examination. Her stepfather told local reporters that shortly before the crash, Filgueiras texted her boyfriend, also a pilot, about the turbulence and ice. The cause of the crash remains undetermined, and the NTSB still expects a preliminary report within about 30 days.

Update — November 6, 2026

On November 4, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office formally identified all nine people killed in the crash, confirming the names the families had released earlier in the week, CBS12 and Boca Daily News reported. The sheriff's office said the identifications were confirmed with the county Medical Examiner's Office and the FBI, that all next of kin have been notified, and that forensic analysis has found no other victims. Recovery work at the site continues. The NTSB has still issued no preliminary report, and the cause of the crash remains undetermined.

Update — November 7, 2026

On Friday, November 6, Allan Filgueiras, the father of co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, spoke publicly for the first time since the crash, at a news conference in Coral Gables, Florida, alongside attorney Stuart Grossman, CNN and the Associated Press reported. Filgueiras, a pilot who taught his daughter to fly, said he has listened to his daughter's final radio transmissions with air traffic control "many times" since the crash, looking for a clue to what brought the jet down — and that what he heard instead was his daughter fighting to keep control of the aircraft to the end. "She's tough," he said. Grossman said the news conference was held to "preserve not just her memory, but her reputation," and that Filgueiras was at the top of her class and perfectly qualified to serve as co-pilot despite her age. Grossman said the family is making no allegations against anyone at this time, has no immediate plans to file a lawsuit, and will wait for the National Transportation Safety Board's findings and have its own experts review them. The NTSB has still issued no preliminary report, and the cause of the crash remains undetermined.

Update — November 9, 2026

In an update dated November 8, 2026, the National Transportation Safety Board said it has completed its on-scene investigative work at the Greenacres crash site except for excavation of the impact crater, which remains ongoing. The board said it has cleared the Green Acres Mobile Home Community, Reading Truck, Silver Oaks Plaza, Value Store It Self Storage, and John I. Leonard High School. Investigators have recovered and identified portions of the aircraft, including components from both wings, both engines, the flight deck, the vertical stabilizer, the horizontal stabilizer, the left elevator, aileron sections, and multiple flap track assemblies, the NTSB said. Some of the recovered parts have been sent to NTSB laboratories in Washington, D.C., for closer inspection. The board again asked anyone who finds debris not to keep, move, or dispose of it, and to contact the NTSB at witness@ntsb.gov, preferably with a photograph. The cause of the crash remains undetermined, and the NTSB has still issued no preliminary report.

Update — November 10, 2026

Investigators have recovered the Learjet's cockpit voice recorder, the National Transportation Safety Board said on Monday, November 9. The recorder was found at the site where the plane first hit the ground, and it is now at the NTSB's laboratory in Washington, where specialists will try to recover the audio from the cockpit in the flight's final minutes, according to The Contrail's November 9 update. The recorder appeared heavily damaged in photos released by the agency, The Contrail reported. Investigators had not previously been able to confirm that a recorder was even on board. The board had said on November 8 that on-scene work was largely complete except for excavation of the impact crater; that excavation is now finished, and residents of the nearby mobile home park can return home, according to The Contrail. Military Trail remains closed between 10th Avenue North and Cresthaven Boulevard. No preliminary report has been issued yet; one is usually expected within about 30 days of the crash.
